title: Your 7-segment is common anode (segment ON = pin LOW). Pattern for digit 1 on a common cathode is 0x06. What do you send now?
explain: A common anode needs the inverted pattern. ~0x06 is 0xF9, and bit 7 (the dp or unused bit) must be masked with 0x7F, so you send 0x79. The cast back to uint8_t avoids the int promotion trap.

title: 5 V, red LED drops 2 V, 220 ohm resistor. How much power does the resistor burn?
explain: Current is (5 - 2) / 220 = 13.6 mA. Power in the resistor is I squared times R, about 41 mW. 68 mW is the whole supply power (5 V times 13.6 mA), not the resistor. A 0.25 W resistor is fine.

title: Cortex-M reset. Word 0 of the vector table is _estack = 0x20020000 (end of RAM). The first push happens. Where is the value stored?
explain: The stack is full descending. PUSH first lowers SP by 4, then writes. So the first word lands at 0x2001FFFC. The address 0x20020000 is just after RAM, so nothing is ever written there.

title: STM32 alternate function for PA9. Which AFR register and which bit shift do you use?
explain: Each pin has 4 bits. AFR[0] (AFRL) holds pins 0 to 7, AFR[1] (AFRH) holds pins 8 to 15. For pin 9: index 9 / 8 = 1, shift (9 % 8) * 4 = 4. Clear the 4 bits first, then set the value.

title: RP2350 bare metal. You write constexpr auto& sio = *reinterpret_cast<SioRegs*>(0xD0000000); What happens?
options: It works and the compiler folds the address
Compile error: reinterpret_cast is not allowed in a constant expression
It compiles, but crashes at run time
explain: A constant expression cannot contain reinterpret_cast, because the compiler cannot treat an integer as an object at compile time. That is why your at<Regs>() helper is a normal inline function, not constexpr. At -O2 it still becomes one load or store.

title: Cortex-M. The TIM ISR (NVIC priority 5) is running. The UART interrupt (priority 2) fires. What happens?
options: UART waits until the TIM ISR returns
Both run at the same time
explain: A lower number means a higher priority. Priority 2 beats priority 5, so UART preempts TIM and TIM continues afterwards. The reverse case (UART running, TIM fires) makes TIM wait. This is the opposite of what many expect.

title: A 16-bit hardware timer wrapped. prev = 65530, now = 5. What does this print?
explain: now - prev is computed as int and gives -65525. The cast to uint16_t reduces it modulo 65536, so you get 11 ticks. Same idea as millis() wrap: always subtract, never compare the two values.

title: clear() never returns on the Uno. Tap the bug.
explain: A uint8_t can only go from 0 to 255. After 255 it wraps to 0, so i < 256 is always true and the loop never ends. Use a wider counter (uint16_t or size_t), or test i < sizeof buf with a type that can hold 256.

title: You debounce a button with R = 10 kohm and C = 10 uF. What is the time constant tau?
explain: tau = R times C = 10 000 ohm times 0.00001 F = 0.1 s = 100 ms. After one tau the capacitor reaches about 63 percent. For a normal button, 100 ms is already slow. A smaller C (100 nF gives 1 ms) is often enough.

pr.title: Remove the useless dummy read
pr.author: dev-anna
pr.body: The read of AHB1ENR after the enable does nothing. Removing it.

explain: The read-back is on purpose. The STM32 errata says the peripheral clock starts 1 to 2 cycles after the write, so an immediate register access can be lost. The dummy read gives a short delay. Keep it and add a comment.
